sections.h2: Where is Papillion, Nebraska, and what kind of city is it?
sections.html:
Papillion is the county seat of Sarpy County and a southwest suburb of Omaha. It began as a railroad town in the 1870s, and today Nebraska Highway 85 runs through its downtown. The city sits at about 1,032 feet above sea level and uses the ZIP codes 68046, 68133 and 68157.

Because Papillion is the county seat, the offices a seller needs are close together. The Sarpy County Treasurer is at 1102 E. 1st Street in Papillion, and City Hall is at 122 E. Third Street. That is a short list of stops for a homeowner who needs a tax receipt, a permit record or a copy of a recorded document before a sale.

sections.h2: How quickly has Papillion grown, and why does it matter for sellers?
sections.html:
Papillion was a small town for its first seventy years and then grew quickly. The census counted 1,034 people in 1950, 5,606 in 1970 and 10,372 in 1990. The city passed 16,000 by 2000 and recorded 24,159 residents in 2020.

With the population more than quadrupling between 1970 and 2020, much of the housing stock was probably built in the last five decades. Sellers of houses from the 1970s through the 1990s should expect buyers to ask about the age of the roof, furnace, water heater and windows.

sections.h2: What is the flood history around Papillion?
sections.html:
Papillion has a documented flood history tied to four streams: Big Papillion Creek, West Papillion Creek, Walnut Creek and Midland Creek. The city's own flood information page says both Big and West Papillion Creek have a record of flooding.

  • August 1959: Big Papillion Creek flooded and six families were evacuated.
  • 1964: the largest flood of record on Big Papillion Creek reached 45,900 cubic feet per second, killed seven people and caused about $5 million in damage, not counting personal property.
  • 1965: a second large flood followed, at 31,200 cubic feet per second.
  • 1993: heavy downpours damaged foundations and retaining walls in the Big Papio Creek watershed.

The Nebraska state flood mitigation plan names June 16, 1964 as the flood of record for Papillion Creek and says the event damaged hundreds of homes in Millard, Ralston and Papillion. The plan adds that the Corps of Engineers built four dams in the watershed and that levees have been added over time, but warns that ongoing development leaves the creeks most vulnerable to flash floods, especially if a levee fails.

sections.h2: What do Papillion flood rules mean for a house sale?
sections.html:
If a house sits in a Special Flood Hazard Area, three things can affect a sale: lender insurance requirements, permits for any work, and a rule about large repairs. Papillion participates in the National Flood Insurance Program and the Community Rating System, so discounted premiums may be available.

  • Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage, and a flood policy has a 30-day waiting period before coverage starts.
  • A property's flood zone comes from the FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map, which lenders use and which the city's Planning Department uses for its overlay rules.
  • An elevation certificate shows whether a building is above or below the base flood elevation.
  • A Floodplain Development Permit is required before building, renovating or grading in the Special Flood Hazard Area.
  • If improvements or repairs cost 50 percent or more of the building's market value, the structure must meet new-building standards, which for a house means the lowest floor, basement included, sits one foot above base flood elevation.

A seller with flood damage who plans a major rebuild should ask the city about that 50 percent threshold before spending money. In some cases, selling the house in its current condition is the simpler path.

sections.h2: What is the weather like in Papillion?
sections.html:
Papillion has four distinct seasons. Weather Channel averages listed for the city show a July daytime high near 87 degrees Fahrenheit and a January nighttime low near 12 degrees, with about 30 inches of precipitation across a year. May is the wettest month at roughly 4.4 inches.

For homeowners that means a furnace that works hard from December through February, a sump pump that matters in spring, and exterior wear from freeze and thaw cycles. A buyer's inspector will test the sump pump, check the basement for moisture and look at the grading around the foundation, so a seller who has dealt with water before should have records ready.

sections.h2: Which schools and employers shape the Papillion market?
sections.html:
Papillion La Vista Community Schools serves the city, and the district reported 12,039 students enrolled in 2023 to 2024 and 1,719 employees. That makes the district one of the area's major employers and a main reason families look for houses here. Because boundaries can change, confirm the school for any address with the district before an offer is made.

Papillion's closeness to Omaha means many residents work elsewhere in the metro area. Our research did not turn up an official list of the largest private employers within the city limits, so we have left that out rather than guess.

sections.h2: How are Sarpy County property taxes paid?
sections.html:
Sarpy County real estate taxes are paid in two installments, with the first half due March 31 and the second half due July 31. The Sarpy County Treasurer accepts payment online, by mail to 1102 E. 1st Street, Papillion, NE 68046, through a secure dropbox outside the 1102 building, or in person at that address. The Treasurer's office left the courthouse and now operates from that building.

The state assessment date is January 1 each year, and residential property is valued at or near 100 percent of actual value. Notices of changed value go out on or before June 1. Before a sale, ask the Treasurer or your title company for the current balance so nothing is left unpaid at closing.

sections.h2: What permits and recording steps come with selling in Papillion?
sections.html:
The city's Building and Fire Safety department issues permits for residential and commercial work, mechanical, electrical and plumbing work, grading, stormwater management, signs and demolition, and it offers an online portal where applicants create an account, submit and pay. An unpermitted deck, finished basement or addition is something a buyer's inspector may flag, so gather permit records before listing or accepting an offer.

The deed is recorded in Sarpy County, and Nebraska's documentary stamp tax applies. The Department of Revenue lists a rate of $3.32 per $1,000 of value, or fraction, on deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026, charged to the grantor. On a $275,000 sale, that is $913. Exemptions exist, so review the state's list if the transfer is a gift or comes through an estate.

sections.h2: What do Papillion sellers commonly face, and where does a cash offer fit?
sections.html: Papillion sellers tend to raise a few issues: a house near one of the creeks with flood insurance questions, a house that needs updates after decades of use, an inherited property that no one in the family wants to keep, or a move that is already scheduled. A cash sale takes loan underwriting out of the process, so the closing date depends on title work, the deed and the Sarpy County recording steps. You can ask for a written offer, compare it against listing the house, and say no at no cost.

faqs.q: When are Sarpy County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due March 31 and the second half July 31. The Sarpy County Treasurer takes payments online, by mail, in a secure dropbox or in person at 1102 E. 1st Street in Papillion. Nebraska charges 14 percent annual interest on delinquent amounts.

faqs.q: Is Papillion in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Parts of the city lie in mapped floodplains along Big Papillion Creek, West Papillion Creek, Walnut Creek and Midland Creek. Check the FEMA flood map for your address through the Sarpy County map service or the Planning Department, since a lender will require flood insurance for a mapped property.

faqs.q: What is the deed tax in Papillion?
faqs.a: Nebraska's documentary stamp tax is $3.32 for each $1,000 of value for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026, and it is imposed on the seller who signs the deed. A $400,000 sale produces $1,328, unless the transfer is exempt.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to repair flood damage in Papillion?
faqs.a: Yes if the property is in the Special Flood Hazard Area. A Floodplain Development Permit is required to build, renovate or grade there, and repairs costing 50 percent or more of the building's value trigger new-building standards.
